name: Tunneling Detection — ICMP, DNS, Telnet & UDP Exfiltration
description: Attackers tunnel data inside legitimate-looking protocols to exfiltrate data or establish C2 while evading network controls. Common tunnel protocols: ICMP (data in payload > 48 bytes), DNS (data in TXT records or long queries), Telnet on non-standard ports, UDP, and IPv6 Telnet. Detection relies on payload size anomalies, unusual record types, and non-standard port usage. Base64 decode extracted data.
source: CDSA Module 08: Intermediate Network Traffic Analysis
notes:
=== ICMP TUNNELING ===
How it works:
  → Attacker appends data to ICMP echo request payload
  → Data hidden in common, often-allowed protocol
  → May be encoded (base64) or encrypted for evasion
  → Normal ICMP data length: ~48 bytes
  → Tunneling ICMP data length: 1000s of bytes (may cause fragmentation)

Detection:
  # Filter ICMP only
  icmp
  
  # Look for large ICMP payloads (tunneling IOC)
  icmp && frame.len > 100    → any ICMP over 100 bytes = suspicious
  
  # Check packet details → ICMP → Data field length
  → Normal: 48 bytes
  → Tunneling: 38,000+ bytes → also triggers IP fragmentation

Inspecting payload:
  1. Right-click suspicious ICMP packet → Packet Details → Data section
  2. Hex dump in Packet Bytes pane (bottom right)
  3. Look for readable text in ASCII column OR base64 pattern
  4. Copy hex/data value → decode in Linux:

# Decode base64-encoded ICMP payload
echo '<BASE64_VALUE>' | base64 -d

# If double/triple encoded:
echo '<BASE64_VALUE>' | base64 -d | base64 -d
echo '<BASE64_VALUE>' | base64 -d | base64 -d | base64 -d

Prevention:
  → Block ICMP outbound (restrictive environments)
  → Inspect ICMP payload content at perimeter (strip or alert on data > 48 bytes)

=== DNS TUNNELING ===
How it works:
  → Data appended to DNS TXT record queries
  → Attacker controls authoritative DNS for their domain
  → Client sends 'TXT query for <encoded_data>.attacker.com'
  → Attacker's DNS server receives data, responds with commands
  → Used for: C2, data exfil, bypassing HTTP/HTTPS proxies, DGA botnets

Detection:
  # DNS traffic
  dns
  
  # Look for excessive TXT record queries from one host
  dns.qry.type == 16    → TXT record queries (type 16)
  
  # High-volume DNS to one external resolver = tunneling or DGA
  → Statistics → Conversations → UDP → sort by packets → one host + dns port = suspect

Inspecting DNS payload:
  1. Filter: dns → find packets with unusual TXT field content
  2. Expand: DNS → Answers → TXT record → data
  3. Right-click data field → Copy → Value
  4. Decode in Linux:

echo '<BASE64_VALUE>' | base64 -d | base64 -d | base64 -d

DNS enumeration IOCs (different from tunneling):
  → Rapid DNS queries for many subdomains = subdomain enumeration
  → ANY query type = full zone info attempt
  → Queries ending with ANY in Info column = suspicious
Filter:
  dns.qry.name contains "<TARGET_DOMAIN>"   → all queries for domain

IPFS DNS/HTTPS tunneling:
  → Watch for DNS/HTTP traffic to cloudflare-ipfs.com or similar IPFS gateways
  → URIs like: https://cloudflare-ipfs.com/ipfs/<CID>
  → Hard to block — peer-to-peer, legitimate CDN domain

=== TELNET TUNNELING ===
How it works:
  → Telnet is cleartext, bidirectional → easy to read and inject
  → Port 23: traditional telnet (still used in legacy systems)
  → Non-standard ports (e.g., 9999): attacker moves telnet to evade port-based detection
  → IPv6: some environments don't monitor IPv6 telnet traffic

Detection — Port 23 (traditional):
  telnet              → Wireshark dissects as telnet protocol
  tcp.port == 23      → show all traffic on port 23
  → Follow TCP Stream → read cleartext commands/data

Detection — Non-standard port:
  tcp.port == <UNUSUAL_PORT>    → e.g., tcp.port == 9999
  → Look for large amounts of TCP from one host on unusual port
  → Follow TCP Stream → check if it looks like terminal I/O
  → Hex/ASCII will reveal 'Telnet' in data field = not legitimate service

Detection — IPv6:
  → Any IPv6 in IPv4-only network = suspicious
  ipv6 && telnet
  ((ipv6.src_host == <SUSPECT_IPv6>) or (ipv6.dst_host == <SUSPECT_IPv6>)) and telnet
  → Follow TCP Stream to inspect content

=== UDP TUNNELING ===
How it works:
  → Attacker uses UDP (connectionless, fast) for data exfiltration
  → No handshake = packets immediately sent
  → Often overlooked vs TCP — fewer controls inspect UDP

Detection:
  udp               → show all UDP traffic
  udp.port == <PORT>  → target specific port
  → Follow UDP Stream (right-click → Follow → UDP Stream)
  → Look for alphabet sequences, encoded strings, or structured data in payload

UDP IOCs:
  → Large consistent UDP payload sizes (not varying like normal VoIP/DNS)
  → One host sending UDP to one destination on one port continuously
  → No DNS traffic preceding the connection (no legitimate service lookup)
  → Unusual destination port (not 53/67/68/161/123 etc.)

Legitimate UDP usage (not tunneling):
  DNS (53), DHCP (67/68), SNMP (161), NTP (123), VoIP, gaming, streaming
